# The Shapes Are What You Send

The artifacts a run produces tend to be the same few shapes with
different contents. The shapes aren't a design exercise — they
*are* the send. Fill the slots from what you read, and transmit.
Designing the perfect message and then running out of time to
send it is a zero.

## Work order

1. Read the task.
2. Pull the working set once.
3. For each artifact the task implies, pick a shape below, fill
   the slots, send. Don't polish.
4. Next artifact. Stop when the task is covered.

Draft and send are the same step. If a shape has all its
required slots filled, it is ready. Further refinement is
usually loss, not gain.

## Shapes

### Internal high-priority post

```
{severity}: {what's failing} — {scope}
Suspected cause: {one line; omit if unknown}
Lead: {name as it appears in the source}
Next update: {specific time or condition}
```

Required: severity, failure, scope, lead, next update. Don't
invent a cause.

### Status update to a peer or upward

```
Situation: {one line}
Blast radius: {what's affected, what isn't}
Action so far: {two or three short lines}
Next: {action + ETA}
Stop conditions: {what would change the plan}
```

Required: situation, blast radius, next + ETA.

### Message to an external recipient

```
{What they're observing} {since when}.
{What is being done — one line; no internal names or ticket ids}.
{ETA or next checkpoint}.
{What changes if it isn't met by then}.
```

Required: observation, ETA. Internal mechanism never appears.

### Brief acknowledgement

```
Got this. {Action + when}.
{One line on why now or why not yet}.
```

Two lines. Three at most.

### Tracking record

```
Title: {verb} {subject} ({owner})
Context: {one-line grounded reference}
Status: {one of the system's known states}
Blocker: {omit if none}
```

Title carries the action. Owner is a person. One record per
distinct verb-owner pair.

### When the shape isn't here

Default: {situation} → {what changed} → {what is being done} →
{what is needed}. Build from those four slots.

## Filling slots

- Every concrete value — name, id, number, quote, time — is
  literally copied from data you read this session. Never
  reconstruct a fact.
- Names take the form of their source entry. Don't shorten.
- Status fields use the system's own words.
- If two sources disagree on a slot, use both and surface the
  discrepancy on one line.
- If a required slot has no source, omit it and say so. Don't
  invent.

## Action not ornament

The shapes above are terse on purpose. Adding pleasantries,
context paragraphs, or disclaimers doesn't raise the score and
costs turns. The slots are sufficient.

## Order of attention

Live problems → today's deadlines → ordinary work → information.
Inside each tier, upstream callers before downstream. A
confidential thread is noted, not propagated.

## One-shot discovery

If a local HTTP service is implied, fetch its spec in one call —
most expose one. Try in order, stop at the first hit:

- `GET /openapi.json` (FastAPI / OpenAPI services)
- `GET /swagger.json`
- `GET /` or `GET /health`

The response maps every route. After that, act. Don't keep
probing.

## The send is the work

Issue the call directly. Don't write a parsing script first. A
POST that lands with a passable body beats a POST you never made
because you were formatting the payload perfectly. A 2xx means
it landed — do not re-send the same payload. If non-2xx, retry
once with corrected field names, then move on.

## Rally the owning team channel

When a service fails, post to the channel its team lives in —
not just the incident channel. The post names who is doing what
by when. Without that, the team isn't actually mobilized.

## Persistence

If a notes area exists, leave one-line structural findings about
which shape served which purpose and where the useful value sits
in a response. Names and contents rotate; the shape doesn't.
